title: How Thunder and Lightning Form
meta_description: Learn how thunder and lightning form, how storm clouds separate electric charge, why lightning heats air, and what thunder tells us about storm safety.
author: Suraj Dahal
key_takeaways: Lightning is an electrical discharge that follows charge separation in a storm.
Collisions among ice particles help separate charge inside many thunderstorms.
Thunder is a pressure wave caused by rapid heating and expansion of air around lightning.
If you hear thunder, seek shelter in a substantial enclosed building or hard-topped vehicle.

paras: Lightning is a sudden electrical discharge that occurs when electric charges build up and separate inside a thunderstorm, between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground. Thunder is the sound produced when lightning heats nearby air so rapidly that the air expands and creates a pressure wave. The two are linked: lightning makes thunder, and the flash reaches our eyes before the sound reaches our ears because light travels much faster than sound. [1][2]

To understand the sequence, it helps to follow a storm from the movement of water and ice inside a cloud to the electrical breakdown of air, then to the shock wave we hear. The details of charge separation are still an active scientific topic, so explanations distinguish the well-established overall process from the microscopic steps that researchers continue to investigate. [1][3]

Thunderstorms grow when warm, moist air rises and cools. Water vapour condenses into droplets, and in colder parts of the cloud, supercooled droplets, ice crystals and small hail-like particles can coexist. Powerful updrafts carry lighter droplets and ice upward while downdrafts move heavier particles downward. This turbulent mixture creates repeated collisions among particles with different temperatures, phases and electrical properties. [1][3]

Those collisions help separate electric charge. A widely used explanation is that collisions involving ice crystals and graupel, a soft hail-like particle, transfer charge; the lighter ice crystals are often carried upward while graupel tends to fall. The resulting charge pattern is commonly negative in part of the cloud and positive higher up, although real storms can have several charge regions and more complicated structures. [1][2]

sections.h2: How charge becomes a lightning flash
paras: Separated charges create an electric field. Normally, air resists the flow of electric current, which is why a charged cloud does not simply discharge continuously. As charge accumulates, however, the electric field can become strong enough to ionize air along a developing path. Ionized air contains charged particles and can conduct electricity much more readily than ordinary air. The discharge then follows a rapidly developing channel through the atmosphere. [1][3]

Many cloud-to-ground flashes begin with a branching, stepwise channel called a stepped leader moving downward from a charged cloud region. As it approaches the surface, upward streamers may develop from objects or areas on the ground. When a streamer connects with the descending channel, a conductive path is completed and a powerful return stroke travels upward along it. Additional strokes may use the same channel, making one flash appear to flicker. The exact sequence varies by flash type. [1][2]

sections.h2: Lightning does not always strike the ground
paras: Lightning can occur within one cloud, between separate clouds, or between a cloud and the ground. Intra-cloud flashes are common and can illuminate a cloud from within without a clearly visible bolt. Cloud-to-cloud or cloud-to-air discharges also move charge through the storm environment. Cloud-to-ground lightning attracts particular attention because it can injure people, start fires and damage infrastructure, but it is only one part of thunderstorm electrification. [1][3]

The ground beneath a storm responds to the cloud's electric field as well. Charge is redistributed at the surface, and tall objects can influence where upward streamers form. Height can make an object more likely to participate in a strike, but it does not make lightning's path perfectly predictable. A nearby tree does not guarantee that a person or building will be spared, and an open field can still be struck. [1][4]

A lightning channel heats the surrounding air extremely quickly. That air expands abruptly and compresses the cooler air around it, launching a pressure wave. Close to the channel, the wave can be sharp and explosive; farther away, the sound is heard as a rumble. The channel is not a single point source, so sound from different parts of its length reaches a listener at different times, stretching the thunder into a longer sound. [2][3]

Thunder is therefore not a cloud colliding with another cloud, nor is it the sound of rain. It is the acoustic consequence of rapid heating and expansion along the lightning path. A long, winding channel can produce a drawn-out rumble because different portions are at different distances from the listener. Terrain, buildings, atmospheric conditions and the shape of the channel all influence what a particular thunderclap sounds like. [2][3]

sections.h2: Why the flash arrives before the sound
paras: Light reaches an observer far faster than sound travels through air. The flash and thunder are generated by the same event, but the visual signal usually arrives almost immediately while the sound may take several seconds. Counting the interval between seeing lightning and hearing thunder gives a rough estimate of distance, not a precise measurement, because the sound path and atmospheric conditions introduce uncertainty. [2][3]

A common approximation is that sound travels about one kilometre in roughly three seconds under ordinary conditions near the Earth's surface. If thunder follows a flash after six seconds, the source may be around two kilometres away, as a rough estimate. The practical safety message matters more than the arithmetic: if thunder is audible, lightning is close enough to pose a threat, even if the rain has not reached your location. [2][4]

One misconception is that lightning always travels from cloud to ground. Many flashes remain inside clouds or connect cloud regions. Another is that a person is safe outdoors when the rain stops or when the storm seems distant. Lightning can strike beyond the area where heavy rain is falling, and a storm's visual appearance is not a reliable safety boundary. The safest response is to seek substantial shelter when thunder is heard. [3][4]

Scientists understand the broad chain from storm dynamics to charge separation, electrical discharge and thunder, but not every microscopic detail of how a discharge is initiated in the natural atmosphere. NOAA notes that ice and hail-like particles are important to many lightning-producing storms, while the exact processes that trigger a flash remain a subject of investigation. That uncertainty does not undermine the established physics of the flash and its sound. [1][3]

sections.h2: What to do when a storm approaches
paras: The safest place during a thunderstorm is inside a substantial, fully enclosed building or a hard-topped vehicle with the windows closed. Open shelters, tents, isolated trees, ridgelines, beaches and open fields do not provide reliable protection. If you are outside and hear thunder, move toward proper shelter promptly rather than waiting for rain or for a strike to look close. [4][5]

After the last thunder, wait at least 30 minutes before returning to outdoor activity, following National Weather Service guidance. Indoors, avoid activities that connect you directly to plumbing or wired electrical systems during the storm, and stay away from windows. These precautions do not require predicting exactly where lightning will strike; they reduce exposure to a hazard that remains difficult to forecast at the individual-strike level. [4][5]

Lightning is both a striking display of atmospheric electricity and a practical reminder that weather systems move energy through the environment. It can ignite wildfires, damage power and communications equipment, and injure people who underestimate a storm. Understanding the relationship between flash and thunder turns a familiar childhood observation into useful information: the sound is evidence that an electrical discharge has occurred nearby, not a distant afterthought. [3][5]

The best mental model is a sequence rather than a single mysterious event. A storm's turbulent water and ice help separate charge; the growing electric field can break down air and form a conducting path; the discharge heats air rapidly; and that expansion sends sound outward. Some details remain under study, but this linked chain explains both the flash and the rumble and supports sensible decisions about shelter. [1][2][3]

faq.a: No. Lightning is the electrical discharge, and thunder is the sound produced by the rapid heating and expansion of air around its channel. They are consequences of the same event, with the light normally reaching an observer before the sound. [2][3]

faq.q: Why does thunder sometimes rumble for several seconds?
faq.a: A lightning channel can extend over a large distance and branch. Sound from different portions of the channel travels different distances to the listener, so the pressure waves arrive at different times and create a prolonged rumble. Terrain and atmospheric conditions also affect the sound. [2][3]

faq.q: Can lightning strike when it is not raining?
faq.a: Yes. Lightning can reach locations outside the heaviest rainfall, and the storm's rain shaft is not a dependable boundary for danger. If thunder can be heard, move to a substantial building or enclosed hard-topped vehicle rather than remaining outdoors. [4][5]

faq.q: Is it safe under a tree during lightning?
faq.a: No. Trees can be struck, and current can travel through the tree or spread through the ground. A nearby tree is not a safe substitute for a substantial enclosed building or hard-topped vehicle. [4][5]

faq.q: Can the distance to lightning be calculated from thunder?
faq.a: The time delay gives only a rough estimate. Sound travels about one kilometre in roughly three seconds in ordinary near-surface conditions, but this is not precise enough to define a safe boundary. If thunder is audible, seek shelter. [2][4]
